pos: adv. (ordinarily; as a general or usual report)
etymology: Latin communis, common, shared by all — what is reported or practiced as the general, usual case.
biblical_def:
So they took the money, and did as they were taught: and this saying is commonly reported among the Jews until this day. It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles.

Both uses of commonly describe a report so widely repeated it has become the default account people reach for, whether or not it is true. Matthew uses it of a lie — the guards' bribed story about the stolen body — kept alive by sheer repetition until it passes, among those who want it to, for settled fact. Paul uses it of a scandal in Corinth so shameless that even the pagans, who tolerated far worse, had no name for it. In both cases commonly is not a defense; a lie commonly reported is still a lie, and a sin commonly known is a sin aggravated, not excused, by its publicity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from COMMON: usually; generally; ordinarily; as a thing of frequent or general occurrence or report.
webster_full: COMMON, a. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely.
COMMONLY, adv. Generally; ordinarily; usually; for the most part.
Applied to what is widely reported, whether the report is true or false.
In Scripture, used once of a persistent lie and once of a notorious sin.
Carries no judgment of truth by itself — only of frequency and spread.
scriptures: So they took the money, and did as they were taught: and this saying is commonly reported among the Jews until this day.
It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife.
corruption_summary: Modern discourse treats what is commonly said as a kind of evidence in itself — if everyone is repeating it, it must carry weight — exactly the error Matthew 28:15 exposes: a lie survives by repetition, not proof.
corruption_paragraphs: The guards' bribed story was commonly reported precisely because repetition was cheaper than refutation; the resurrection could not be disproved, so the alternative was simply repeated until it sounded established. Common report is not common truth.

Paul's use cuts the other way: a sin commonly known in the church is worse for being commonly tolerated, not better for being commonly discussed. A culture that measures scandal by how openly it is named, rather than by whether it is repented of, has inverted Corinthians.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew or Greek root; the Greek sense in both texts is carried by verbs of report (diaphemizo-type spreading) rather than a technical term.
roots_lines: Commonly describes the spread of a report, not its truth.
Matthew 28:15 shows a lie kept alive by repetition alone.
1 Corinthians 5:1 shows a sin aggravated, not excused, by publicity.
The word measures frequency, never accuracy.
Both texts warn against mistaking wide report for settled fact.
usage: Commonly reported among the Jews — a lie sustained by repetition.
Reported commonly that there is fornication — a sin worsened by its publicity.
Scripture never treats common report as proof of anything.

pos: adv. (recently; freshly; lately come into being or into a state)
etymology: Old English niwlice, from niwe, new — of a thing or state only just arrived.
biblical_def:
So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.

The word newly marks the precise moment of Gideon's advantage. Midian's watch had only just been changed — the new guard not yet alert, the old guard not yet gone — and it is into that exact seam of confusion that three hundred men blow trumpets and smash pitchers. Nothing in the text credits the timing to Gideon's cleverness; the narrative has already told the reader that the army was reduced to three hundred precisely so that Israel could not claim the victory as its own doing. Newly set the watch is a small, almost administrative detail, and that is the point: God's providence governs even the changing of a pagan guard.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from NEW: lately; freshly; not long since; recently come into existence or into a particular condition.
webster_full: NEW, a. Not old; lately made, invented, or produced.
NEWLY, adv. Freshly; recently; not long ago.
Marks the precise recency of an event or change of state.
Used in Judges of a watch only just changed.
Carries no moral weight in itself — only precise timing.
scriptures: Jdg 7:19

So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.
corruption_summary: Nothing about newly set the watch is corrupted in common usage; the entry preserves a small providential detail that is easy to read past in a famous battle narrative.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is a plain marker of timing, not a theological term under attack.

The principle worth recovering is attentiveness to small details of timing in narrative Scripture: the newly changed watch is not decoration but the hinge of the account, a reminder that providence often works through unremarkable administrative facts rather than visible miracles.
roots_summary: Hebrew narrative detail without a distinct technical term; the force is carried by the whole clause describing the state of Midian's watch.
roots_lines: Newly marks the precise recency of the watch's change.
Gideon's three hundred strike at the exact seam of the changeover.
The reduced army was already set apart so the victory could not be claimed by Israel.
Small administrative timing becomes the hinge of the whole battle.
Providence governs details as unremarkable as a changed guard.
usage: Had but newly set the watch — the precise moment of Midian's vulnerability.
Gideon's three hundred strike into that exact seam.
A reminder that providence works through unremarkable timing.

pos: adv. (in detail; point by point; specifically rather than in general)
etymology: Latin particula, a small part — to treat a matter part by part rather than as a whole.
biblical_def:
And when he had saluted them, he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry. And over it the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat; of which we cannot now speak particularly.

The two uses sit in deliberate tension. Paul in Jerusalem declares particularly — item by item — what God had done among the Gentiles, because the elders needed the specific evidence to settle a specific controversy. The writer to the Hebrews refuses to speak particularly of the mercy seat and the cherubim, not from ignorance but from restraint: some sacred furniture is described enough to establish its reality and its typology without becoming an object of idle curiosity. Scripture is particular exactly where particulars serve the argument, and reticent exactly where they would not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PARTICULAR: in detail; specifically; distinctly, one point at a time rather than in sum or general statement.
webster_full: PARTICULAR, a. Pertaining to a single person or thing, as distinguished from others.
PARTICULARLY, adv. In a particular manner; specially; distinctly; individually.
Used of detailed, itemized report, as opposed to summary.
In Acts, of Paul's detailed account of Gentile ministry.
In Hebrews, of a deliberate refusal to elaborate further.
scriptures: And when he had saluted them, he declared particularly what things God had wrought among the Gentiles by his ministry.
Heb 9:5
And over it the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat; of which we cannot now speak particularly.
corruption_summary: A culture addicted to exhaustive disclosure treats every refusal to elaborate as evasion, missing Hebrews 9:5's example of disciplined restraint — particulars are not owed merely because they are wanted.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 21:19 models particularity rightly used: Paul gives the Jerusalem elders exactly the detail their question required, because the controversy over Gentile inclusion needed specific, checkable evidence, not a vague assurance.

Hebrews 9:5 models the opposite discipline. The writer could say more about the mercy seat but chooses not to, trusting that the main argument does not require it. Modern discourse, suspicious of any unexplained detail, rarely permits itself that kind of restraint.
roots_summary: Greek kath hekaston-type phrasing (one by one) underlies the Acts usage; no single technical Hebrew or Greek root governs both texts.
roots_lines: Particularly means detail given point by point, not in summary.
Paul uses it to answer a specific controversy with specific evidence.
Hebrews refuses it where elaboration would not serve the argument.
Scripture is particular where particulars help and reticent where they would not.
Disclosure is a tool for the argument, not an end in itself.
usage: Declared particularly what God had wrought — detailed, itemized testimony.
Of which we cannot now speak particularly — deliberate, disciplined restraint.
Scripture is as particular, and as reticent, as its argument requires.

pos: adv. (in agreement with what is just; correspondingly; in due proportion)
etymology: From ACCORD, Latin cor, heart — to be of one heart or measure with a standard, hence to answer in due proportion.
biblical_def:
According to their deeds, accordingly he will repay, fury to his adversaries, recompence to his enemies; to the islands he will repay recompence.

Accordingly is the hinge word of divine justice in this verse: it names the exact correspondence between what a man has done and what he receives. There is no excess and no shortfall in the Lord's repayment — deeds on one side of the scale, recompense on the other, matched without remainder. The verse reaches past Israel's borders to the islands, the farthest Gentile peoples, insisting that this proportioned justice is not a tribal privilege but the character of the Judge of all the earth. Accordingly leaves no room for the comfortable thought that distance from Israel is distance from accountability.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ACCORD: agreeably; in agreement with something previously stated; correspondently; in due proportion to a standard.
webster_full: ACCORD, n. Agreement; harmony of mind; consent; concurrence of opinion.
ACCORDINGLY, adv. Agreeably; suitably; in a manner conformable to something else.
Used of exact correspondence between cause and consequence.
In Isaiah, of God's repayment matched precisely to deeds.
Extends divine justice beyond Israel to the furthest Gentile peoples.
scriptures: According to their deeds, accordingly he will repay, fury to his adversaries, recompence to his enemies; to the islands he will repay recompence.
corruption_summary: Therapeutic moral language prefers outcomes loosely proportioned to feeling rather than deed, but Isaiah 59:18 insists that God's repayment is exactly accordingly — matched to what was actually done, not softened by circumstance or distance.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture suspicious of exact retribution tends to flatten accordingly into something vaguer — consequences as a general tendency rather than a precise match. Isaiah will not allow the flattening: deeds on one side, recompense on the other, without remainder.

The reach to the islands matters: it forecloses the comfortable assumption that distant peoples are outside the ledger. Accordingly is universal in scope precisely because it is exact in measure — the same God who repays Israel's adversaries repays the furthest Gentile sin just as precisely.
roots_summary: Hebrew keghemuwl, according to the deed or recompense, the standard term for exact retributive measure in prophetic justice oracles.
roots_lines: Accordingly names exact correspondence between deed and consequence.
Isaiah pictures repayment matched to deeds without remainder.
The reach to the islands universalizes the scope of divine justice.
Distance from Israel is not distance from accountability.
The word forbids both excess and shortfall in judgment.
usage: According to their deeds, accordingly he will repay — exact retributive measure.
Fury to his adversaries, recompence to his enemies — matched without remainder.
To the islands he will repay recompence — justice reaching the farthest Gentile.

pos: adv. (wisely; with practical discretion and foresight)
etymology: Latin prudens, contracted from providens, foreseeing — to act with the foresight that sees what a situation requires.
biblical_def:
Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high.

This single word opens the fourth Servant Song and sets its whole trajectory: exaltation follows from prudent dealing. But the prudence Isaiah describes is not political shrewdness — the chapters that follow immediately describe a servant despised, rejected, and acquainted with grief, whose exaltation comes only through suffering. Prudently therefore names a wisdom that accepts the Father's appointed path even when it runs through humiliation, trusting that exaltation lies on the far side of it rather than apart from it. The Servant's prudence is obedience all the way down, not calculation that avoids the cross.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PRUDENT: wisely; discreetly; with judicious foresight and practical wisdom in the conduct of affairs.
webster_full: PRUDENT, a. Wise in the conduct of affairs; discreet; cautious; practical.
PRUDENTLY, adv. In a prudent manner; with wisdom and discretion.
Implies foresight that governs action toward a right end.
In Isaiah, opens the fourth Servant Song immediately before the Servant's suffering is described.
Names an obedience that accepts a hard path as wise, not merely a shrewd avoidance of difficulty.
scriptures: Behold, my servant shall deal prudently, he shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high.
corruption_summary: Modern usage treats prudence as risk-avoidance, the opposite of Isaiah's sense, where the Servant's prudence leads directly into suffering before it leads to exaltation.
corruption_paragraphs: If prudence means avoiding cost, Isaiah 52:13 is a contradiction: the Servant deals prudently and is immediately described, three verses later, as having no form or comeliness, despised and rejected. Scripture's prudence absorbs cost rather than evading it.

The corrective is to read prudently as wisdom toward the Father's appointed end, not wisdom toward personal comfort. Christ's prudence was obedience unto death, and his exaltation followed precisely because he did not deal prudently by the world's definition.
roots_summary: Hebrew sakal, to be wise, prosper, act with insight — the same root rendered elsewhere as prosper or give good success, binding wisdom to outcome under God's hand.
roots_lines: Prudently opens the fourth Servant Song of Isaiah.
The Servant's exaltation is tied directly to his prudent dealing.
The following verses describe suffering, not shrewd self-preservation.
Biblical prudence can mean obedience through humiliation, not around it.
Exaltation in Isaiah 52-53 follows suffering; it does not replace it.
usage: My servant shall deal prudently — wisdom bound to the Father's appointed path.
He shall be exalted and extolled, and be very high — exaltation following obedience.
Prudence here absorbs cost rather than avoiding it.

pos: adv. (with sound judgment; circumspectly; wisely in speech or action)
etymology: Latin discretus, separated, discerned — the ability to discern rightly between things, hence to speak or act with careful judgment.
biblical_def:
And when Jesus saw that he answered discreetly, he said unto him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God.

The scribe in question had just named the two great commandments — love of God and love of neighbor — as greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices, and Jesus answers that discreet reply with real commendation. Discreetly here is not mere cleverness; it is a correct ordering of the law's weight, placing love above ritual without abolishing ritual's place. Yet not far from the kingdom is a pointed warning alongside the praise: sound discernment about the law is not the same as entering the kingdom. The scribe saw rightly and still stood outside, a reminder that right answers are necessary but never sufficient without the submission they describe.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISCREET: with sound judgment and prudence; circumspectly; wisely, so as to avoid error or excess.
webster_full: DISCREET, a. Prudent; wise in avoiding errors or evil, and in selecting the best means to accomplish a purpose.
DISCREETLY, adv. With discretion; prudently; judiciously.
Implies correct discernment, not merely cleverness.
In Mark, of a scribe's correct ordering of the law's commands.
Commended by Christ, yet paired with a warning that discernment alone does not save.
scriptures: And when Jesus saw that he answered discreetly, he said unto him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God. And no man after that durst ask him any question.
corruption_summary: A culture that equates having the right opinion with spiritual arrival misses Mark 12:34's warning: the scribe answered discreetly and was told only that he was not far from the kingdom, not that he had entered it.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to treat sound doctrinal discernment as the finish line, especially where correct answers are prized. Jesus commends the scribe's discreet answer and in the same breath keeps the kingdom's door still ahead of him.

The corrective is not to despise discretion — the scribe was right to rank love above sacrifice — but to refuse the substitution of right answers for personal submission to the King those answers describe.
roots_summary: Greek nounechos, having sense, sensibly, a rare New Testament word used only here, naming intellectual soundness rather than emotional tact.
roots_lines: Discreetly names sound discernment, not mere cleverness.
The scribe correctly ranked love above ritual sacrifice.
Jesus commends the answer while keeping the kingdom still ahead of the man.
Right discernment about the law is necessary but not sufficient for entrance.
No man after that durst ask him any question — the exchange closes debate, not discipleship.
usage: He answered discreetly — sound, correct discernment about the law.
Thou art not far from the kingdom of God — commendation paired with warning.
Right answers describe the King; they do not replace submission to him.

pos: adv. (fittingly; with propriety; in a manner suited to good order)
etymology: Latin decens, fitting, becoming — what is suitable and orderly, as opposed to what is crude or chaotic.
biblical_def:
Let all things be done decently and in order.

This short verse closes Paul's long correction of Corinthian worship, where prophecy, tongues, and eager speakers had turned the assembly into competing voices rather than edifying worship. Decently names the positive standard he sets against that chaos: not suppression of spiritual gifts, which he has just spent a whole chapter regulating rather than forbidding, but their exercise within a shape that serves the whole body. In order is decently's inseparable partner — order is not opposed to the Spirit's work but is how the Spirit's work is received without confusion. The verse governs far more than first-century tongues; it is Scripture's own standard for how any corporate worship ought to be conducted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DECENT: fitly; suitably; in a manner becoming and proper; with propriety of behavior or arrangement.
webster_full: DECENT, a. Becoming; suitable; fit to be seen; proper in manner, dress, or language.
DECENTLY, adv. In a decent manner; with propriety; suitably.
Governs corporate conduct, not merely individual behavior.
In 1 Corinthians, the closing standard for regulated worship.
Paired inseparably with in order, Scripture's own definition of proper worship.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Worship culture often polarizes between rigid formalism and unstructured spontaneity, both missing 1 Corinthians 14:40's actual standard, which regulates spiritual gifts without silencing them.
corruption_paragraphs: Some read decently and in order as license for cold, unfeeling formalism, ignoring the twelve chapters before it that assume living spiritual gifts in the assembly. Order was never meant to replace the Spirit's work, only to shape it.

Others read spontaneity itself as more spiritual, treating any structure as quenching the Spirit. Paul regulates, rather than forbids, precisely because unregulated gifts had produced confusion that edified no one. Decently and in order is the corrective to both errors at once.
roots_summary: Greek euschemonos, becomingly, and taxis, order — the same pairing used elsewhere of a well-ordered military rank, applied here to the assembly of the church.
roots_lines: Decently names propriety and fittingness, not coldness.
In order is its inseparable partner in Paul's standard.
The verse closes a chapter regulating, not forbidding, spiritual gifts.
Order serves the whole body rather than suppressing individual gifts.
This is Scripture's own definition of rightly ordered corporate worship.
usage: Let all things be done decently and in order — the closing standard for worship.
Order shapes the Spirit's work rather than replacing it.
Neither cold formalism nor unregulated spontaneity answers to this verse.

pos: adv. (with firm assurance; boldly affirming without wavering)
etymology: Latin confidens, from con- and fidere, to trust fully — to speak from a trust so settled it admits no hesitation.
biblical_def:
And about the space of one hour after another confidently affirmed, saying, Of a truth this fellow also was with him: for he is a Galilaean.

The irony of this confidently is total: a bystander in the high priest's courtyard presses Peter with complete, unwavering certainty — and is entirely right. Peter answers that correct confidence with his third denial, this time with cursing and swearing. Confidently here belongs not to the apostle's faith but to a stranger's accurate observation, a reminder that unwavering assurance is not itself a virtue; it is only as good as the truth it serves. The rooster that crows immediately after exposes the gap between the stranger's calm confidence and Peter's collapsing nerve.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONFIDENT: boldly; with firm trust or assurance; without hesitation or doubt.
webster_full: CONFIDENT, a. Having full belief; trusting; having strong assurance.
CONFIDENTLY, adv. With confidence; without wavering; boldly.
Describes the manner of an assertion, not its truth.
In Luke, used of a bystander's accurate accusation of Peter.
Highlights the gap between calm human confidence and Peter's panic.
scriptures: And about the space of one hour after another confidently affirmed, saying, Of a truth this fellow also was with him: for he is a Galilaean.
corruption_summary: Confidence is often treated today as a virtue regardless of content, but Luke 22:59 shows confident speech belonging to an accurate stranger while the apostle answers it with a third, cursing denial.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-assurance culture prizes the tone of confidently affirmed statements over their truth. Luke's narrative supplies a corrective by accident of placement: the confident speaker here is simply correct, and confidence adds nothing to that correctness except emphasis.

The real drama is Peter's, not the bystander's. Three denials, escalating to cursing and swearing, show that unwavering inward resolve (I will not deny thee, though I should die with thee) is worthless without grace to sustain it in the moment of pressure.
roots_summary: Greek diischurizeto, to assert strongly or insist, a verb of forceful affirmation rather than a technical theological term.
roots_lines: Confidently describes the manner of speech, not its truth.
The bystander's confident accusation of Peter is entirely accurate.
Peter answers accurate confidence with his third, cursing denial.
Human assurance is only as valuable as the truth it serves.
The cock's crow exposes the gap between resolve and grace.
usage: Another confidently affirmed — a stranger's accurate, unwavering accusation.
Of a truth this fellow also was with him — confidence paired with correctness.
Peter's resolve collapses where grace alone could have sustained him.

pos: adv. (sorrowfully; with a heavy or troubled countenance)
etymology: Old English saed, sated, weary — originally meaning grave or serious, narrowing over time to sorrowful.
biblical_def:
And he asked Pharaoh's officers that were with him in the ward of his lord's house, saying, Wherefore look ye so sadly to day?

Joseph asks this question of two fellow prisoners, Pharaoh's butler and baker, whose troubled faces betray dreams they cannot interpret. Sadly here describes a visible heaviness that a sold, forgotten, imprisoned man notices in others before attending to his own far greater cause for sorrow. The question itself is the first recorded act of the Joseph who will later weep over his brothers and provide for a starving world: he reads the grief of men who hold his fate in their hands, and uses the gift God has given him not for himself but to serve them. Sadly marks the opening of the chapter that leads, however slowly, to Joseph's exaltation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SAD: sorrowfully; with a grave, heavy, or dejected countenance; mournfully.
webster_full: SAD, a. Sorrowful; mournful; heavy in countenance or spirit.
SADLY, adv. In a sad manner; sorrowfully; with a dejected look.
Describes visible countenance, not merely inward feeling.
In Genesis, noticed by Joseph in his fellow prisoners.
Marks the start of the chain of events leading to Joseph's exaltation.
scriptures: Gen 40:7
And he asked Pharaoh's officers that were with him in the ward of his lord's house, saying, Wherefore look ye so sadly to day?
corruption_summary: Nothing about Joseph's question is corrupted in modern usage; the entry recovers a small, overlooked act of attentiveness in a man with every reason to be consumed by his own grief.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is a plain description of visible sorrow, not a theological term under cultural pressure.

The principle worth recovering is Joseph's outward attentiveness in the depth of his own injustice. A man sold by his brothers and forgotten in prison still notices, and asks after, the sadness of men beneath him — the same pattern of other-directed care that marks his conduct throughout the narrative.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra, bad or evil, idiomatically rendered sadly in the phrase literally your faces are evil today, i.e., troubled or ill at ease.
roots_lines: Sadly translates a Hebrew idiom for a troubled countenance.
Joseph notices the sadness of men who hold his fate in their hands.
His question begins the chain of events leading to his exaltation.
Outward attentiveness marks Joseph even in the depth of injustice.
The gift of interpretation is first used to serve others, not himself.
usage: Wherefore look ye so sadly to day — Joseph's attentiveness to others' grief.
Asked while Joseph himself remained forgotten and imprisoned.
The question opens the chapter that leads to his exaltation.

pos: adv. (at a measured, unhurried pace; without haste)
etymology: Old English slaw, sluggish, dull — originally of dullness or laziness, narrowing to describe mere pace.
biblical_def:
And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone.

Luke's precise travel log of Paul's voyage to Rome includes this unglamorous detail: contrary winds, many days, barely making headway. Slowly is not a spiritual metaphor here but a sailor's honest report, and that honesty matters for the chapter's larger argument. The storm that follows this slow beginning will nearly destroy the ship, and an angel will promise Paul that every soul aboard will be saved — a promise that holds true even though the journey itself, start to finish, was marked by delay, danger, and difficulty rather than smooth providence. Slowly reminds the reader that God's guidance of Paul to Rome did not bypass ordinary hardship; it worked through it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SLOW: with a moderate or unhurried pace; not swiftly; tardily; after a measured passage of time.
webster_full: SLOW, a. Not swift; moving with little speed; tardy.
SLOWLY, adv. In a slow manner; not quickly; gradually.
Used literally of a ship's pace against contrary wind.
Opens Luke's extended account of Paul's voyage and shipwreck.
Marks providence working through, not around, ordinary difficulty.
scriptures: Act 27:7
And when we had sailed slowly many days, and scarce were come over against Cnidus, the wind not suffering us, we sailed under Crete, over against Salmone;
corruption_summary: A results-oriented spirituality tends to read slow progress as a sign something has gone wrong, while Acts 27 pairs a slow, difficult voyage with God's unconditional promise that every soul aboard would be saved.
corruption_paragraphs: Sailed slowly many days opens a chapter that only gets harder — storm, shipwreck, loss of cargo, loss of hope among the crew. If slow and difficult progress were evidence against God's guidance, this voyage would disprove it immediately.

Instead Luke's careful, almost tedious detail of delay and danger sets up the angel's promise in verse 24 all the more starkly: God's plan to bring Paul to Rome was never contingent on an easy journey. Slowly is not a sign of abandoned providence but simply what providence often looks like from inside the ship.
roots_summary: Greek braduploeo, a rare compound verb (slow-sailing), used nowhere else in the New Testament, naming the literal, technical difficulty of sailing against the wind.
roots_lines: Slowly describes a literal, technical sailing difficulty, not a metaphor.
It opens Luke's detailed account of Paul's voyage to Rome.
The voyage that follows includes storm and shipwreck.
An angel's promise of safety holds despite, not instead of, the hardship.
Providence here works through delay and danger rather than around them.
usage: We had sailed slowly many days — literal difficulty against contrary wind.
Opens the chapter that leads to storm and shipwreck.
Slow, hard providence is still providence.
